About: The Nonlinear Pendulum — When the Textbook Formula Breaks

Source

Simulation
Nonlinear pendulum "ghost race": the true sin θ dynamics (RK4-integrated) swings alongside a ghost obeying the small-angle formula, plus a T(θ₀)/T₀ elliptic curve with a slider-bound static marker.
Concept
T = 2π√(L/g) is an approximation that ignores amplitude. The exact period grows with release angle — only ~0.05% high at 5°, +7.3% at 60°, +18% at 90° — following the complete elliptic integral K.
Serves
Limits of the SHM idealization: reading the textbook period as the θ₀ → 0 limit; judging where linearization is trustworthy.
Inquiry
Predict whether a wider swing takes more, less, or the same time; release at 10° then 90° and watch the ghost separate; count laps until the ghost leads by a full swing.
Misconception
"The period is independent of amplitude" — true only as θ₀ → 0. Encoded as prediction choice B; rebuttal shown only when chosen.
Verified anchors
L = 1 m, g = 9.81 m/s²: T₀ = 2.0061 s; 5° → 2.0071 s (×1.0005); 60° → 2.1529 s (×1.0732); 90° → 2.3678 s (×1.1803). Computed here by the same AGM iteration used for every displayed number.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet the ghost race

Solid bob: the true dynamics — angular acceleration θ̈ = −(g/L)sin θ. Dashed ⚠ ghost: the textbook formula T₀ = 2π√(L/g), which is blind to the release angle. Both start from rest at the same release angle θ₀ (L = 2 m). Held at release until you press ▶.

2 · Predict — wide vs gentle

Same pendulum, two releases from rest: a gentle 10° and a wide 90°. One complete swing (out and back) at 90° takes…

3 · Watch at θ₀ = 10°

The ⚠ ghost hugs the real bob. Its period is the shorter one, so it creeps ahead — by only ~0.2% of a swing per lap, as the Ghost lead readout shows. Near θ₀ → 0 the textbook formula is trustworthy.

4 · Race at θ₀ = 90°

Both re-released at 90°. Count laps until Ghost lead in the Race readout reaches a full swing (it turns red). Each real lap costs +18% — the formula’s lead compounds.

5 · Read the T(θ₀) curve

The flat amber line is the formula’s claim: the same T for every amplitude. The cyan curve is the exact period — they touch only as θ₀ → 0, and by 90° the real period is already +18%.

6 · What the formula ignores

Change L at fixed θ₀: both periods stretch by √L together — the ghost’s lead per lap doesn’t change. Amplitude, not length, is what T₀ forgets.

The Physics

The Nonlinear Pendulum — When the Textbook Formula Breaks · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Textbooks give a pendulum's period as T₀ = 2π√(L/g), a formula with no release angle in it. This sim swings a real pendulum next to a dashed formula bob that follows T₀ exactly, so you can test the formula.

What you'll learn

  • Where T₀ = 2π√(L/g) comes from, and what it assumes.
  • How the period of the real pendulum depends on the release angle θ₀ and the length L.
  • How to read the period off the T/T₀ curve.
Both bobs start together, from rest, at the same angle θ₀ on a string of length L.

What's on screen

  • Solid cyan bob: the real pendulum, obeying the true equation.
  • Dashed amber bob: swings exactly as the formula says.
  • Readouts: the real period, and the Race card with laps and the Ghost lead in swings.
  • 📈 T(θ₀) curve: opens beside the pendulum, showing T/T₀ against release angle.
See itHold both bobs at a release angle of 30°. Watch for: a solid cyan bob with a dashed amber ring around it, both at the release angle.

03

The textbook formula replaces sin θ with θ

Gravity's pull back along the arc is proportional to sin θ, so the real bob obeys

d²θ/dt² = −(g/L) sin θ
The true equation of motion.

For small angles, with θ in radians, sin θ ≈ θ (at 10° they differ by 0.5%). The equation becomes simple harmonic motion, whose period has no θ₀ in it:

d²θ/dt² = −(g/L) θ, T₀ = 2π√(L/g)
The textbook shortcut.

The dashed bob follows this version exactly, θ = θ₀ cos(√(g/L) t). The solid bob follows the sin θ equation, which has no closed form in elementary functions, so the sim computes it step by step.

Key idea. T₀ is only as accurate as sin θ ≈ θ.
See itRelease at 10°. Watch for: the dashed bob staying close to the real bob through the first swings.
04

The real swing takes longer than the formula

  • On either side of the vertical, |sin θ| < |θ|, so the real pull back is weaker than the formula assumes.
  • A weaker pull builds up speed more slowly, so the real bob takes longer to swing down and across than the dashed bob does.
  • The wider the release, the bigger the gap, and the longer the swing.
release θ₀real swing longer bydashed bob is a full swing ahead after
10°0.2%≈ 524 laps
30°1.7%≈ 57 laps
90°18%≈ 5.5 laps

One lap is one full swing, out and back: one period. At L = 2 m, T₀ = 2.837 s, and the real period is 2.842 s at 10° and 3.349 s at 90°.

See itRelease both bobs from 90°. Watch for: the Ghost lead on the Race card growing by about 0.18 swing every lap.
05

The exact period is T₀ times a factor set by θ₀

The real period has no formula in elementary functions. It is T₀ times a correction factor that depends only on θ₀:

T = T₀ · (2/π) K(sin(θ₀/2))
K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, a standard special function that the sim evaluates for you.
θ₀5°30°60°90°
T / T₀1.00051.01741.07321.1803

For small θ₀ in radians, T/T₀ ≈ 1 + θ₀²/16: double a small amplitude and the extra time grows four times. This is good to about 30°, and at 90° it gives 1.154 against the true 1.180. As θ₀ nears 180° (almost upside down) the period grows without limit. The sim stops at 90°.

See itOpen the T/T₀ curve for a 60° release. Watch for: the cyan (real) curve rising above the flat amber line, with a marker at 60°.
06

Length sets the time scale, the angle sets the error

In T = T₀ × (factor set by θ₀), the length appears only inside T₀ = 2π√(L/g).

  • Length sets the time scale. T₀ grows as √L, so going from 1 m to 3 m stretches every period by √3 ≈ 1.73.
  • The release angle sets the error. T/T₀ has no L in it, so the dashed bob's lead, counted in swings, is the same at any length.
  • The extra time per swing is the same fraction at any length. At 90°, each swing is 18% longer than T₀. That is 2.37 s against 2.01 s at 1 m, and 4.10 s against 3.47 s at 3 m.
See itRace from 60° with a second pendulum of 3 m beside one of 1 m. Watch for: the readouts T₁ = 2.15 s and T₂ = 3.73 s, a ratio of 1.73.
07

Where it matters

  • Pendulum clocks. A clock is set for its usual swing. If the swing size drifts, its rate drifts too: a change from 2.0° to 2.2° costs about 1.4 s a day. This is called circular error, and it is why clock swings are kept small and steady.
  • Huygens, who built the first pendulum clock, added curved guides (cycloidal cheeks) that shorten the string on wide swings. On a cycloid the period does not depend on the amplitude at all.
  • Measuring g. Timing a pendulum gives g, but a 10° swing already makes the answer about 0.4% too small unless you correct for it.
08

Summary

In one line. The textbook period T₀ = 2π√(L/g) rests on an approximation. This sim measures how much that approximation costs at each release angle.

Key points

  • T₀ = 2π√(L/g) comes from replacing sin θ by θ.
  • Since sin θ < θ, every real swing is longer than T₀, and more so at wider angles.
  • The real period is T₀ times a factor that depends only on θ₀.
  • Length sets the time scale. The release angle alone sets the error.

Common mix-ups

  • "The period doesn't depend on amplitude." That holds only for very small swings.
  • "A wide swing is quicker, because the bob moves faster." The bob does move faster. It also covers a longer arc, and the pull back is weaker than the formula assumes.
  • "A longer pendulum makes the error worse." The error as a fraction of T₀ does not depend on L.

Things to try on your own

  • Set θ₀ to 45° and count the laps until the Ghost lead reaches one full swing. Compare with 25 laps from the T/T₀ factor.
  • Turn on Second pendulum with L₂ = 1 m against L = 3 m, and compare the two periods.
